notes.text: garden tomb, as if they existed at this spot right here, the holy mount. So that when we say that Solomon's temple was an epic temple, in many ways it was the epic temple of all temples, because it was designed to pull together all of the symbolism of the atonement into one place. Therefore the concept when you say Jerusalem or when you say Zion, or when you say holy mountain or holy mount, it all appears to refer to all of the events that deal with the atonement and they all culminate in the place in the temple.

Isaiah ties several things together. He ties the garden of Gethsemane, which sits right here, and he ties Golgotha (i.e. Calvary), and the garden tomb, which sit over here. They become tied as if they are part and partial of the temple itself, because the temple mount commands the whole area. Therefore, Isaiah appears to deal with this whole complex, Zion, Jerusalem, Gethsemane, Mount of Olives, Golgotha,

quotes.text: Jehovah plays a very active role in the events of the earth, including those that will occur during these last days and at his second coming, as set forth in this section. He will make a feast for all people (although only the meek and humble of the earth will attend), "destroy . . . the veil that is spread over all nations," he will "swallow up death in victory," "wipe away tears from off all faces," and take away the "rebuke of his people." After we have partaken of the Lord's feast, and after he has wiped away our tears, we will worship him with these words (25:9): Lo, this is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us: this is the Lord; we have waited for him, we will be glad and rejoice in his salvation. Note that with these words we will twice testify "this is our God/Lord," twice affirm "we have waited for him," and twice speak of his salvation ("save us"/"salvation").
quotes.speaker: Donald W. Parry
